progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: Year 11: carbon has four valence electrons and forms four covalent bonds; single, double and triple covalent bonds; drawing simple molecules with lines for bonds; molecular formulas. Not assumed: any IUPAC rule, skeletal formulas, the words parent chain, locant, substituent, saturated, unsaturated. No earlier Year 12 video is assumed (route entry knowledge).
progression.startsWith: Identify the parent chain and bond type. The video opens: The canister under this camping stove holds butane, often mixed with propane. That name isn't a brand. It's a code: but means four carbons, and ane means only single bonds between them.
progression.stopsAfter: drawing a hydrocarbon three ways and counting implied hydrogens; naming straight and branched alkanes, alkenes and alkynes up to C8 with methyl and ethyl branches (longest chain, nearer-end numbering, di- and alphabetical order, multiple-bond locant and priority); drawing a structure from a name and checking its molecular formula by counting. No isomers (chem-m7-c02), no shapes, bond angles, general formulas or homologous series (chem-m7-c03), no other families, no safety.
progression.nextLesson: the same atoms can be joined in different ways (route chem-m7-c02, "How can the same formula make different molecules?").

teaching.task: A name like 3-methylpent-1-ene looks like a code. How do you read a name like that, write one from a drawing, and draw the molecule back from the name?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a name such as butane is a code for a structure (1); (2) carbon forms four bonds and bonds to other carbons, so chains and branches give millions of compounds, and each needs a name that points to one structure; real chains zigzag (2); (3) three drawings, and the four-bond rule that restores implied hydrogens (3); (4) the stem counts carbons (4); (5) the ending shows the bonds, so it tells you whether the chain is saturated (5); (6) the longest chain is the main chain, traced even round a bend, because a branch drawn hanging down can be part of it (6); (7) branches are named by their carbons, and numbering from the nearer end gives the lowest locants (7); (8) several branches: di- and alphabetical order (8); (9) a double or triple bond must be in the main chain and gets a locant before the ending (9); (10) the multiple bond wins the numbering (10); (11) names reverse into structures, checked by counting (11); memory aid (12); two attempts and brief feedback (13 to 16); handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: the camping gas canister holds butane, and the name is a code (but means four carbons, ane only single bonds), so the video asks how to read a name like 3-methylpent-1-ene, write one from a drawing and draw the molecule back from the name. Carbon's four bonds explain chains and branches; one chain is drawn three ways (full structural, condensed, skeletal); the naming rules then come one at a time: the stem counts the carbons in the longest continuous chain, even round a bend; the ending shows the bonds (saturated ane, ene, yne); branches are named with yl and the chain is numbered from the end nearer the branch; several branches take di and alphabetical order with commas and hyphens; a double or triple bond must be in the main chain and wins the low numbers. Reading 2,2-dimethylpentane back into a skeletal formula shows names work both ways, and the memory aid gathers the order: longest chain with the multiple bond, number it, then write the name. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: The canister under this camping stove holds butane, often mixed with propane. That name isn't a brand. It's a code: but means four carbons, and ane means only single bonds between them. Chemists name carbon compounds this way, so a name like three-methylpent-one-ene is really a set of drawing instructions. So how do you read a name like that, and write one from a drawing?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "The skeletal formula of a hydrocarbon is shown. Give its IUPAC name and its molecular formula." Structure: 5-methylhex-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH(CH₃)CH₃, drawn skeletal (zigzag of six with the double bond second from the left end and a methyl branch on the fifth carbon). New compound, tests the longest chain containing the double bond, double-bond priority and implied-hydrogen counting. Crossed mistake: "2-methylhex-4-ene" (numbered for the branch). (A2) "A student names a hydrocarbon '2-ethylpentane'. Explain why this name is incorrect. Give the correct IUPAC name and draw the skeletal formula of the compound." Answer 3-methylhexane (site A2 item 1's compound, reached by a new route). Tests the longest chain and nearer-end numbering. Crossed mistake: "4-methylhexane" (wrong end).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate the nomenclature of organic chemicals, up to C8, using IUPAC conventions, including simple methyl and ethyl branched chains, including: (ACSCH127); alkanes; alkenes; alkynes; alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary); aldehydes and ketones; carboxylic acids; amines and amides; halogenated organic compounds" This video covers the first three examples (alkanes, alkenes and alkynes) with methyl and ethyl branches. The other families are named in the videos that teach them (see Open decisions on the route mapping). this video starts from the parent chain and bond type and stops at naming and drawing simple branched alkanes, alkenes and alkynes up to C8. It teaches: carbon's four bonds let it form chains and branches (Year 11 callback), so each compound needs a name that points to one structure; real chains zigzag, which is why skeletal formulas zigzag; full structural, condensed and skeletal formulas, and counting implied hydrogens (end carbon three, corner two, branch point one; scene 9 adds that a C=C counts as two bonds, so each of its carbons has one fewer hydrogen); rule 1, the stem counts the main chain's carbons (meth to oct); rule 2, the ending shows the carbon to carbon bonds (-ane, -ene, -yne), with saturated and unsaturated given plain meanings; rule 3, the longest continuous chain, which may bend on the page; branch names (methyl, ethyl) and rule 4, numbering from the nearer end (locant); rule 5, several branches (di-, commas and hyphens, alphabetical order ignoring di-); double and triple bonds (the main chain contains the multiple bond, the locant sits before the ending, no locant for ethene or propene); the multiple bond wins the numbering over a branch; reading a name back into a structure and checking the molecular formula by counting. Not here: structural isomers (chem-m7-c02, the next video; 2-methylbutane and pentane appear only as separate examples, never compared as isomers); bond angles and shapes (tetrahedral, trigonal planar, linear), general formulas CnH2n+2, CnH2n, CnH2n−2 and homologous series (chem-m7-c03, which owns C7-IQ2-01); physical properties; functional-group families beyond hydrocarbons (alcohols in chem-m7-c05, carbonyls in chem-m7-c08b, acids in chem-m7-c09, amines and amides in chem-m7-c11, haloalkanes with their reactions); cycloalkanes (one appearance in chem-m7-c02); safe handling and disposal (C7-IQ2-05, the P videos' risk tables, route review change 5); "first point of difference" tie-breaks and substituent-numbering subtleties beyond the cases shown.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; the main chain highlighted pale blue by the tracer; branches amber; the double or triple bond teal; locant numbers small navy; the name builder's slots: branches amber, stem pale blue, ending teal (matching what each part describes). Board layout (constant): top-left the short task line or rule chip ("Rule 3 of 5: longest chain"); centre the structure board, one molecule at a time; bottom the name builder strip; a plate sits small at the right only in the hook and handoff. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous worked case leaves the board before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plate `m7-camping-gas-burner-v1.png` (inspected 21 Oct: a lit blue camping stove on a blue unlabelled gas canister, silver pot supports, brass valve, blue flame; no person or hand, no text; 2000 × 2000; hook and scene 17's callback, small, never stretched). Considered, not used: `m7-crude-oil-barrel-v1.png` (inspected: a plain dark steel drum; it carries no naming idea here and belongs to chem-m7-c03), `m7-ethanol-fuel-bottle-v1.png` (inspected: an amber stoppered bottle of pale liquid; used in chem-m7-c02). No new plates. No human figures.
design.transitionPlan: The camping gas burner plate opens the hook as the name splits into its coded parts; the board clears to one carbon with four bond lines that joins into a chain and a branch; butane draws full, condensed and skeletal in a row; each naming rule gets its own rule chip (Rule 1 of 5 to Rule 5 of 5) as the stem ladder, the three two-carbon bond skeletons, the bent chain with the chain tracer painting the longest path pale blue, the locant counter running from the nearer end and the amber branches with the name builder slots write in turn; the double bond scenes draw teal bonds inside the traced chain and the counter compares both ends; the name builds back into a skeletal formula one part at a time with hydrogens checked; the memory aid writes three handwritten lines, earlier lines dimming; each attempt clears the board and its feedback traces the chain and fills the name builder under the question card; the name builder ticks each slot as the butane formula question hands off; scene crossfade with settle.
